cues.text: Chapter nine is an independent case-analysis practice.
Here you stop learning the pieces one at a time and apply them together to a single scenario, the way you would in an examination or in professional work.
Here is the scenario.
A fictional online retailer discovers that a support export containing customer addresses was publicly accessible for two days.
Notice what the facts tell us and what they leave open.
There is an export, produced from a customer support system.
It contains customer addresses.
It was publicly accessible, and it stayed that way for two days.
What the scenario does not tell us is whether anyone actually opened or downloaded the file, who the people were if they did, or what they did with it.
Hold on to that gap, because the source makes it central to the analysis.
The source gives you a case method, a sequence of steps.
Let us walk through them in order.
First, identify stakeholders and facts.
Stakeholders are the people and organisations with an interest in the outcome.

Here that includes the customers whose addresses were in the export, the retailer itself, the support staff who created or handled the export, and any vendor or service provider involved in the support system.
Facts are what you can establish: what the export contained, how it became publicly accessible, when it began and ended, and how long it lasted.
The scenario already gives us two days.
Second, determine personal data and legal scope.
Ask whether the customer addresses are personal data, and which data protection law or laws apply to this retailer and these customers.
Remember that regulatory scope differs from one regime to another, so you must determine which one covers the situation rather than assume it.
This is also where you separate an ethical question from a legal one.
A duty to customers may exist ethically even where you have not yet shown that a particular law applies, and you should not treat a general ethical principle as a legal requirement.
Third, contain and preserve evidence.
Containment means stopping the exposure, so that the export is no longer publicly accessible.
Preserving evidence means keeping the records that will let you understand what happened, such as access records and the details of the export itself.
These two aims must be handled together.
If you simply delete everything in a panic, you may end the exposure but destroy the information you need to answer the next question.
Fourth, assess actual access and risk.
This is the step that addresses the gap we noted at the start.
Being publicly accessible is not the same as being accessed.
You must work out whether the export was in fact accessed, by whom where that can be known, and what risk that creates for the customers whose addresses were in it.
Fifth, check controller and processor duties and deadlines.
Recall that the controller decides the purposes and means of processing, while a processor handles personal data on the controller's behalf.
In this case you ask which role the retailer holds, which role any vendor holds, what each must do, and whether any notification deadlines apply.
Deadlines matter because breach obligations, where they apply, run against the clock.
Sixth, communicate protective actions where required.
Where the law or sound ethical practice calls for it, tell affected customers what happened and what they can do to protect themselves.
The words "where required" are a qualification you must preserve.
Not every incident demands the same communication, and your analysis should justify when it does.
Seventh, improve export access, retention and vendor governance.
This is the lesson-learning step.
Examine who could create and reach exports, and how access was controlled.
Examine retention, meaning how long such exports were kept.
And examine vendor governance, meaning how the retailer oversees the vendors involved in its support operations.
Now the source sets the standard for a good answer.
A reasoned analysis must do three things.
First, it must state what is unknown.
Honest analysis names its uncertainties instead of filling them with guesses.
Second, it must avoid claiming that every disclosure caused harm.
Exposure creates risk, but whether harm actually followed is a separate question, and you should not assert it without support.
Third, it must justify actions with legal and ethical principles.
Every step you recommend should be tied to a reason, whether a legal obligation, an ethical principle, or both, and you should keep those two kinds of reason distinct.
The source adds one last note about this exercise.
It is an independent exercise, not the graded final case.
Use it as practice, and treat it as a chance to rehearse the method.
The chapter closes with a checklist of what you must be able to explain before examination.
You should be able to explain the difference between privacy and security.
Privacy concerns appropriate handling of personal information, while security concerns protecting it, and this case touches both.
You should be able to explain each regulatory scope, meaning which law applies to whom and where.
You should be able to explain lawful basis, the legal justification for processing personal data, and rights exceptions, the circumstances in which individual rights may be limited.
You should be able to explain mapping, which is knowing what personal data you hold and where it flows.
You should be able to explain the DPIA, the data protection impact assessment.
You should be able to explain minimisation, collecting and keeping only what is needed, and privacy by design, building protection in from the start.
You should be able to explain breach thresholds, the point at which an incident triggers obligations.
And you should be able to explain accountability, being able to show that you comply, and vendor oversight, the duty to supervise those who process data for you.
As a final exercise, take the retailer scenario and walk through the seven steps in order.
At each one, write what you know, what you do not know, and which principle justifies your action.
